item.title: Was the early universe really as pristine as scientists thought?
item.description: Astronomers long imagined the young cosmos as a nearly empty place made of hydrogen and helium. New James Webb Space Telescope observations show some early galaxies were already spreading carbon, oxygen, and silicon — the stuff of planets and living things — just 500 million years after the Big Bang.

item.title: What Does Northern Ireland's New Plan to Bring Nature Back Actually Promise?
item.description: Northern Ireland just launched a long-term Nature Recovery Strategy to restore habitats and halt biodiversity loss — here's what it sets out to do, and why it matters far beyond one corner of the map.

item.title: How Did a Spacecraft Use Earth as a Slingshot to Reach Jupiter?
item.description: A European spacecraft on its way to Jupiter just swung past Earth at 8,640 km above the Indian Ocean — borrowing our planet's gravity to speed up without burning precious fuel.

item.title: How Did Thousands of Strangers Buy a Whole English Estate?
item.description: A 9,500-acre slice of English countryside went up for sale for the first time in centuries — so 25,000 ordinary people chipped in to buy it together and hand it back to nature.

item.title: How Did Antarctica's First Dinosaur Bone Hide in a Drawer for 40 Years?
item.description: A small fossil collected on an icy Antarctic island in 1985 sat forgotten in a museum drawer for four decades — until a curious scientist opened it and realised it was the first dinosaur bone ever found on the continent.

item.title: What Makes a Golden Eagle Chick Called Beaky Junior So Important?
item.description: A young golden eagle named Beaky Junior has become the first chick to fledge from a managed grouse moor in southern Scotland — and his flight marks a comeback three centuries in the making.

item.title: Could a Reusable Spaceplane Really Fly to Space Twice a Day from a British Airport?
item.description: Spaceport Cornwall and New Zealand firm Dawn Aerospace have signed an agreement to explore flying a reusable, runway-launched spaceplane from Newquay — a sleek rocket-powered craft that could one day reach the edge of space and be back on the ground in time to do it all again the same day.

item.title: Could a Nuclear Clock Keep Time Better Than Any Clock Ever Built?
item.description: Deep inside a crystal of thorium, scientists in Vienna have built the world's first self-stabilizing nuclear clock — a device that keeps its own rhythm and is so accurate it would drift by just one second over 30 million years.

item.title: How Did a Cooler Summer Give Japan Its Best Potato Harvest in a Decade?
item.description: While heat and drought shrank harvests across much of the Northern Hemisphere, one cool, rainy island in northern Japan pulled off its finest potato crop in ten years — a reminder of how much good farming depends on the weather.

item.title: What Happens When Two Dead Stars Collide and Make a Brand-New Magnetar?
item.description: When two dead stars crashed together more than six billion years ago, they flashed with X-rays for nearly ten minutes — far longer than usual. Astronomers think the collision may have left behind a newborn magnetar, one of the strangest objects in the cosmos.

item.title: How Steady Is NASA's New Planet Hunter — Steady Enough to Hit a Dime From 150 Miles Away?
item.description: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has proven it can hold its aim almost perfectly still — and its special 'star-shade' camera has just caught its first light from another galaxy.

item.title: How Did a Texas School Custodian Get an Elementary School Named After Her?
item.description: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton kept a Texas school district running — and quietly did far more than clean. When a brand-new elementary school needed a name, the community chose hers.

item.title: Why Do Quarks Leave Ripples in the Universe's Very First Soup?
item.description: In the first millionths of a second after the Big Bang, the universe was a blistering soup of quarks and gluons. Now physicists at CERN have watched a single quark drag ripples through that ancient matter — proof it really did flow like a liquid.

item.title: Why Are People Deliberately Making Their Clothes Look Mended?
item.description: Instead of hiding a tear, a growing number of people are stitching bright stars, felt animals and bold patterns right over it. The fashion world is paying attention.

item.title: Can the Human Heart Really Handle the Trip to Mars? A New Study Says Yes
item.description: Thirteen astronauts spent six months in space, and researchers found their hearts adapted well enough to handle the weaker gravity of Mars. Regular exercise, it turns out, may be the secret.

item.title: Why Did Crocodiles Survive the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs?
item.description: A new study of more than 7,000 fossils suggests crocodiles and their relatives outlasted the dinosaurs by doing something simple and clever — they kept moving toward warm places, and the tropics stayed livable when much of the planet did not.

item.title: How Did Scientists Listen to 98 Million Bat Calls Across England's Woodlands?
item.description: Researchers hung tiny microphones in 310 English woodlands and recorded bat calls for nearly 10,000 nights. The result is one of the biggest wildlife listening projects ever attempted — and it found some of Britain's rarest bats hiding in plain sound.

item.title: Why Did Crocodiles Survive the Asteroid That Ended the Dinosaurs?
item.description: When the asteroid struck 66 million years ago, most dinosaurs vanished — but crocodiles and their relatives lived on. A new study of 7,000 fossils suggests their love of warm places put survivors exactly where the climate stayed kind.

item.title: How Did Astronauts Give the ISS a Powerful Solar Upgrade?
item.description: Two astronauts spent over 7 hours outside the International Space Station, installing a new solar array that will boost the station's power by up to 30%.

item.title: Can Floating Islands Be Entire Cities?
item.description: On Lake Titicaca in Peru, the Uros people have been building entire floating cities out of totora reeds for generations — proving that a floating home can be more than just a house.
